name: Kingdom of Dagbon
info: The Dagomba kingdom of northern Ghana, founded by Naa Gbewaa and built by Naa Nyagsi's 15th-century conquest of the earth priests, ruled from Yendi and trading with Hausaland until the German conquest of 1896.

facts.capital: Pusiga under Naa Gbewaa; Yani Dabari near Tamale under Naa Nyagsi; Yendi (Yani) after the Gonja wars
facts.founder: Naa Gbewaa, by the Lunsi's histories; his grandson Naa Nyagsi (r. 1416–1432) conquered the Tindaamba and organised the state
facts.predecessor: The decentralised Dagomba towns (Tinsi) under their earth priests, the Tindaamba; the migrant line of Tohazhie from east of Lake Chad, Mali and Biun in Gurma
facts.successor: German Togoland (Eastern Dagbon, 1896) and the Northern Territories of the British Gold Coast (Western Dagbon); reunited under British mandate after the First World War; a traditional kingdom within Ghana since 1957

t: The Lunsi, the drummer-historians of the court, trace the royal line to Tohazhie the Red Hunter, who left Tunga east of Lake Chad for Zamfara and Mali, and to Naa Gbewaa, who settled at Pusiga and whose children founded Mamprugu, Nanung and, through his daughter Yennenga, the Mossi kingdoms.

Naa Nyagsi (r. 1416–1432) overthrew many of the Tindaamba, the earth priests who had led the Dagomba towns, set his sons, brothers and uncles over the conquered peoples and made his capital at Yani Dabari; the surviving tindaamba kept their ritual office.

At the Battle of Adibo in 1896 about 7,000 Dagomba with bows and arrows charged a German force of 100 well-armed men under Valentin von Massow, Hans Gruner and Gaston Thierry; it was a massacre, Yendi was destroyed and the Gbewaa Palace burnt.
dyk: Dagbon's scholars of the house of Moliyili wrote in a modified Arabic script, lexically Arabic but syntactically Dagbani; their manuscripts on law, pilgrimage, medicine and metallurgy were burned in the German invasion, and much of what survived was carried to Denmark in the twentieth century.
ev: In the fifteenth century Naa Gbewaa unifies the Dagomba and related peoples ruled by the Tindaamba and settles at Pusiga, where he rules until he goes blind; his grave is there.
Naa Nyagsi wages a war of expansion, overthrows many of the Tindaamba and establishes his capital at Yani Dabari near Tamale.
Yendi, the capital since the Gonja wars, is said to be bigger than Kumasi and Salaga.
Dagbon is placed in the neutral Salaga Area, from Yeji to Yendi, agreed between the Germans and the British to forestall conflict.
The Germans defeat the Dagomba at the Battle of Adibo, destroy Yendi and burn the Gbewaa Palace; Eastern Dagbon falls to German Togoland.
Yaa Naa Andani II dies in August; the British and Germans split Dagbon between German Togoland and the Gold Coast.
On 7 April Friedrich Rigler's German expedition attacks the Dagomba who had fled to Sang in British territory, kills at least 83, among them Andani's son Idi, and installs Alasan as Yaa Naa.

sections.foundation:
Dagbon was settled long before it was a kingdom. Archaeology shows farming and iron working in the Neolithic, and the aboriginal Dagomba, the Dagbon Sablisi, lived in a decentralised society of towns, Tinsi, each headed by a tindana, an earth priest who pacified the tingbana, the earth gods, the bina and the buga. The royal line came from outside. The Lunsi tell of Tohazhie, the Red Hunter, who left Tunga east of Lake Chad with a small band of horsemen for Zamfara in present-day Nigeria and then Mali, where he married Pag Wabiga, daughter of the king, and fathered Kpoginumbo. Driven south by reprisals from the rising Songhay Empire, Kpoginumbo seized power at Biun in Gurma, and his son Naa Gbewaa left Biun to settle at Pusiga in the north-east corner of Ghana.

Gbewaa unified the small states of the Tindaamba and ruled at Pusiga until he went blind. His sons Tohagu and Gmantambo founded Mamprugu and Nanung, and his daughter Yennenga went north to marry Rialle, whose son Ouedraogo founded the Mossi kingdoms. After Gbewaa's death his children under Shitobu settled briefly at Gambaga and moved south to Namburugu near Karaga, where the king took the title Yaa Naa, 'king of strength'. Shitobu's son Naa Nyagsi (r. 1416–1432) waged a war of expansion, overthrew many of the Tindaamba, set his sons, brothers and uncles over the conquered Konkomba, Nafeba, Basare and Chamba, and made his capital at Yani Dabari near Tamale.
sections.socioeconomy:
Dagbon lies in the Guinean forest–savanna mosaic, with wet and dry seasons, and holds the largest iron ore reserve in Ghana. Trade made Yendi. Naa Zanjina, remembered as the first Muslim Yaa Naa, encouraged commerce, and with the capital settled at Yendi and peace restored a Muslim community grew at the palace: Dyula of Mande origin under the Sabali-Yarna and Hausa Muslims under the Kamshe Naa. Their trade linked Dagbon with the Fezzan, Egypt and the Bight of Benin, and the kingdom exchanged salt and kola nuts with the Mossi kingdoms, the Mali and Songhai empires and the Hausa Bakwai. By 1788 Yendi was said to be bigger than Kumasi and Salaga.

Learning was an industry of the court. The scholarly house of Moliyili, supported by the Yaa Naa with material resources and granted administrative and legal independence, wrote chronicles, biographies, jurisprudence, pilgrimage guides, Arabic grammar and Qur'anic commentary, and works on agriculture, medicine, pharmacology and metallurgy, in the Dagbanli script, a modified Arabic hand that Phyllis Ferguson describes as lexically Arabic and syntactically Dagbani; the kingdom counts Moliyili as the oldest institution of learning in Ghana. The Lunsi, the drummers under the Namo Naa, preserved history and genealogy in recited and drummed proverbs. Women held wealth and office: titles such as the Gundo Naa were reserved for them, and they ruled male subjects and owned royal lands.
sections.military:
The army of Dagbon is the Sapashina. Naa Nyagsi's war of expansion in 1416–1432 made the kingdom, overthrowing the earth priests and holding sway over the Konkomba, Nafeba, Basare and Chamba. Its hardest wars were with the Gonja, whose attacks on western Dagbon, Tomo, and especially on Daboya, did great damage; Naa Luro defeated them in a later battle but could not withstand the sustained warfare and moved the capital east from Yani Dabari, the 'ruins of Yani' near Diare, to the present Yani, Yendi. The Gonja followed, until Naa Zanjina decisively defeated them and killed their chief Kumpatia at Sang near Yendi.

Dagbon's well-organised and powerful army let it resist colonisation when the Germans pressed from the east, the British from the south and the French from the north. The Germans failed to take Dagbon in several attempts; from their point of view Yaa Naa Andani II had disturbed the trade road from the coast to their station at Sansanné-Mangu. In 1896 Valentin von Massow, Gruner and Gaston Thierry met the Dagomba at the Battle of Adibo: about 7,000 poorly equipped Dagomba rushed with bows and arrows at 100 well-armed Germans, and it was a massacre. Yendi was destroyed, its valuables carried off and the centuries-old Gbewaa Palace burnt. In 1900 Friedrich Rigler's expedition found Yendi deserted, crossed into British territory and on 7 April attacked Andani's son Idi and his followers at Sang, killing at least 83.
sections.governance:
The king of Dagbon is the Yaa Naa, whose court sits at Yendi. Naa Nyagsi built the state by installing his sons, brothers and uncles as rulers over the conquered peoples, and the kingdom is divided into territorial chiefdoms from divisional to village level; the gate chiefdoms of Karaga, Savelugu and Mion are reserved for sons of former Yaa Naas, and holding one qualifies a prince to contest the Nam at Yendi, while lesser chieftaincies go to grandsons. Succession has always rotated among the royal houses, once three, Andani Yili, Aburi Yili and Mahami Yili, now the two houses of Abudu and Andani. Governance joins the chiefs with the Tindaamba: the earth priests survived Nyagsi's conquest as ritual mediators between the people and the gods of the land, and every town still has its tindana.

Women hold chieftaincies of their own, a rarity in Africa: the Gundo Naa heads all female chiefs and the Zosimli Naa makes alliances and friendships. From Naa Zanjina, the first Muslim ruler, Muslim elders entered the political structure, the Sabali-Yarna and later the Kamshe Naa saying the Yaa Naa's protective prayers, with titles such as the Walgu Naa, who saw that the king had his portion to 'drink the Qur'an', the Nayil Liman and the Yidan Kambala. Under German and then British rule the Yaa Naa remained at Yendi, but imperial interference in the succession has left the kingdom with repeated disputes.
sections.impact:
Dagbon was a mother of kingdoms. From Naa Gbewaa's children came Mamprugu and Nanung, and through his daughter Yennenga the Mossi kingdoms of Ouagadougou, Tenkodogo, Yatenga and Fada N'Grumah, whose people are nearly half of Burkina Faso and who honour her as their mother; the Bouna kingdom of Ivory Coast and the Dagaaba states of Ghana's Upper West also came out of Dagbon. At its height the kingdom covered the Northern, Upper West, Upper East, Savannah and North East regions of present-day Ghana and parts of Burkina Faso, north-eastern Ivory Coast and north-western Togo, and Islam entered northern Ghana through its court and the Dyula and Hausa merchants it welcomed.

Its intellectual legacy is singular in the region: the scholarly house of Moliyili, a writing system of its own, the Dagbanli Ajami script, and centres of healing, with chieftaincies held by women. Dagbon is called the oldest and one of the most organised traditional kingdoms in Ghana, and since independence in 1957 it has held the customary role of the country's other kingdoms. The loss was also great: colonial conquest took its artefacts and its manuscripts, the Moliyili archives burned, others shipped to Denmark, and the partition of 1899 divided a people whose wounds, by their own account, did not fully heal until the second decade of the twenty-first century.
sections.decline:
The scramble for West Africa closed on Dagbon from three sides. In 1888 the British and Germans made a neutral zone, the Salaga Area from Yeji to Yendi; in 1896 the Germans broke it at Adibo, destroyed Yendi and burnt the Gbewaa Palace, and Eastern Dagbon passed to German Togoland while Western Dagbon became a protectorate, not a colony, of the British Gold Coast. In 1899 the two powers formally split the kingdom, leaving the Yaa Naa at Yendi under German rule and cut off from his people in the west. When Andani II died in August 1899 the succession fell into dispute; Governor August Köhler backed Alasan, Na of Karaga, and after Rigler's troops killed at least 83 of Idi's party at Sang on 7 April 1900 Alasan was installed.

After the First World War Eastern Dagbon became British mandated territory and was reunited with the west. The British ruled through the chiefs and imposed a head tax that sent Dagomba to the southern mines and cocoa farms to earn it. Since Ghana's independence in 1957 Dagbon has been a traditional kingdom, but the imperial meddling in its succession from the 1920s left disputes that have cost lives: troops were sent to Yendi after Yaa Naa Mahama II died in 1954, and in March 2002 Yaa Naa Yakubu Andani II was murdered with forty-two of his elders in fighting by supporters of the Abudu house. A committee of three eminent chiefs settled the conflict in 2018, and on 18 January 2019 the kingmakers elected Yaa Naa Abubakari Mahama.

summary: The Kingdom of Dagbon was built by Naa Gbewaa's line in the fifteenth century, when Naa Nyagsi conquered the earth priests of the Dagomba towns. Ruled by the Yaa Naa from Yendi, it traded with Hausaland and the Sahel, schooled scholars at Moliyili and mothered the Mossi kingdoms, until the German massacre at Adibo in 1896 and the partition of 1899.
references: Martin Staniland, The Lions of Dagbon: Political Change in Northern Ghana (Cambridge University Press, 1975)
Phyllis Ferguson, Islamization in Dagbon: A Study of the Alfanema of Yendi (PhD thesis, University of Cambridge, 1973)

pointDescs.1400: Naa Gbewaa unifies the Dagomba under the Tindaamba from Pusiga in the fifteenth century; his children found Mamprugu, Nanung and the Mossi kingdoms.
pointDescs.1416: Naa Nyagsi begins his war of expansion, overthrowing many of the Tindaamba and installing his kin over the conquered peoples.
pointDescs.1432: Nyagsi's reign ends with the kingdom organised from his capital at Yani Dabari near Tamale, the surviving tindaamba kept as earth priests.
pointDescs.1500: The kingdom founded in the fifteenth century holds the north; the Gonja wars that later force the capital east to Yendi lie ahead, undated in the traditions.
pointDescs.1700: Yendi is the capital after Naa Luro's retreat and Naa Zanjina's victory over the Gonja at Sang, reigns the traditions do not date; Zanjina, the first Muslim Yaa Naa, fosters trade and a Muslim community at the palace.
pointDescs.1788: Yendi is said to be bigger than Kumasi and Salaga; Dyula and Hausa trade links the kingdom to the Fezzan, Egypt and the Bight of Benin.
pointDescs.1888: The Germans and British set up the neutral Salaga Area from Yeji to Yendi; Dagbon, with a well-organised army, resists colonisation from three sides.
pointDescs.1896: The German massacre at the Battle of Adibo: Yendi destroyed, the Gbewaa Palace burnt, Eastern Dagbon taken into German Togoland.

notes: The article dates only Naa Nyagsi (r. 1416–1432), 1788, 1888, 1896, 1899, 1900 and the twentieth century; the Gonja wars, Naa Luro, Naa Zanjina and the move to Yendi are undated. The points 1500 and 1700 are placeholders for that undated middle, and their descriptions say so; the editor may prefer to drop them (leaving six points, below the guide's minimum).
Register start 1400: the article says 'founded in the 15th century'. End 1896: the article's Adibo; the partition (1899) and the Sang killings (1900) follow in the events and the decline section.

Spellings vary in the article (Tohaʒee/Tohazie/Tohazhie, Kpuɣnambo/Kpoginumbo/Kpogonumbo, Nyaɣsi/Nyagsi, Shitobu/Sitobu, Yennenga/Yemtori, Gmantambo/Ŋmantambu, Tindaamba/Tindaanima): the Latin forms are used.

'Ghana's first female minister and Africa's first female cabinet minister', 'the University of Moliyili', 'Ghana's oldest learning institution' and 'largest iron ore reserve' are the article's claims, repeated as such; they are not independently checked.
The military section's '7,000 Dagomba against 100 Germans' and 'massacre' are the article's words; German casualties are not given there.
No references: the article's reference list is empty; Phyllis Ferguson is named without a title.
